title: Hitchhikers Guide to the Internet
summary: Offers hints to new network participants on how the direction of the Internet is set, how to find online information, and how to be a good neighbor on the network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1118 is a guided tour of the Internet as it was in 1989. It explains where the Internet came from, who ran it, how a packet found its destination, how names were turned into addresses, and what the author thought was going wrong.

questions: what is the hitchhikers guide to the internet
why is rip limited to 15 hops
subtitle: A guided tour of the Internet as it stood in 1989.

tldr.problem: The Internet of 1989 was large, distributed and hard to get oriented in. Newcomers needed to know who ran it, where the standards lived, how packets found their way and how names turned into addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1118 is a guided tour. It explains the origins of the Internet, the organizations that ran it, how RFCs are written and classified, the routing protocols in use, the domain name system, and the problems the author saw, including the quirks of the then-current Unix systems.
tldr.outcome: The document is a snapshot of a specific moment. It also appends a list of the major RFCs considered necessary to understand the Internet and contact points for the network information services, and it is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Networks the Internet was designed for

today: RFC 1118 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It describes the Internet as it stood in 1989, and its appendices list the major RFCs it considered necessary to understand the Internet, together with contact points for the network information services.

sections.title: What the Internet Is and Who Runs It
sections.content:
In the beginning there was the ARPANET, a wide area experimental network connecting hosts and terminal servers together. Procedures were set up to regulate the allocation of addresses and to create voluntary standards for the network. As local area networks became more pervasive, many hosts became gateways to local networks, and a network layer to allow those networks to inter-operate was developed and called the Internet Protocol. Over time other groups created long haul IP based networks, and those interoperate too because of IP. The collection of all of these interoperating networks is the Internet.

A few groups provide much of the information service. The Information Sciences Institute does much of the standardisation and allocation work, acting as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. SRI International provides the principal information services by operating the Network Information Center, and after you are connected most of the information in the document can be retrieved from there. BBN provides information services for CSNET and NSFNET, and Merit provides information services for NSFNET.

Each network has its own operations centre. The ARPANET is run by BBN under contract from the Defense Communications Agency, and its facility is called the Network Operations Center. Merit operates NSFNET from a separate centre, and the regional networks have similar facilities to monitor their portion of the Internet. If a problem comes up, the document suggests that a campus network liaison should contact the network operator to which he is directly connected, rather than trying to trace the problem further up.

The Network Information Center is available to all Internet users by network, telephone and mail, with network access being the most common. Interactive access is used to query service overviews, look up user and host names and scan lists of documents. A separate group of addresses handles general assistance, user registration, hostname and domain changes, computer operations and comments on the center's own publications.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet grew out of a research network, and the part that made it work everywhere was a common network layer, IP. Several organisations ran the pieces and kept the registries, and each network had its own operations centre to answer for it.

sections.title: The RFCs and How They Are Classified
sections.content:
The internal workings of the Internet are defined by a set of documents called RFCs. The general process for creating one is for someone wanting something formalised to write a document describing the issue and mail it to Jon Postel, who acts as a referee for the proposal. It is then commented on by all those wishing to take part in the discussion, and it may go through multiple revisions. Should it be generally accepted as a good idea, it is assigned a number and filed with the RFCs.

There are two independent categorisations of protocols. The first is the state of standardisation, which is one of standard, draft standard, proposed, experimental or historic. The second is the status of the protocol, which is one of required, recommended, elective or not recommended. A protocol is expected to move from elective to required as it moves from proposed to standard.

A Required Standard protocol, such as the Internet Protocol itself, must be implemented on any host connected to the Internet. Recommended Standard protocols are generally implemented by network hosts, and the lack of them does not preclude access to the Internet but may affect its usability. The Transmission Control Protocol is given as an example of a Recommended Standard. Elective Proposed protocols were discussed and agreed to, but their application never came into wide use, whether because there was no wide need or because a technically superior idea ran against other pervasive approaches. The document suggests that where a site does need such a facility, an implementation done in accordance with the RFC is worthwhile, so that the work is generally usable should its time come.

Informational RFCs contain factual information about the Internet and its operation, with Assigned Numbers given as an example. Finally, as the Internet and the technology have grown, some RFCs have become unnecessary. These obsolete RFCs cannot be ignored, however, because when a change causes a new RFC to be issued that obsoletes others, the new RFC may hold only the explanation and motivation for the change. Understanding the model on which the whole facility is based may involve reading the original and subsequent RFCs on the topic.

Only a few RFCs actually specify standards; most are for information or discussion. To find out what the current standards are, the document points to the RFC titled IAB Official Protocol Standards, most recently published as RFC 1100.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write an RFC and mail it in. If the idea is good it gets a number and people argue about it in public. The number says nothing about importance, so the series also carries a separate label for how far along a protocol is.

sections.title: How a Packet Finds Its Way
sections.content:
Routing is the algorithm by which a network directs a packet from its source to its destination. The document compares this to a small child trying to find a table in a restaurant: an adult sees the layout of the room and picks an optimal route, but the child is presented with a set of paths between tables where a good path, let alone the optimal one, is not discernible.

IP gateways, more correctly called routers, are boxes with connections to multiple networks that pass traffic between them. They decide how a packet is to be sent based on the information in the IP header and on the state of the network. The header information used is primarily the destination address; other information such as type of service is largely ignored. The state of the network is determined by the routers passing information among themselves, and the distribution of that database, the form of the updates and the metrics used to measure the value of a connection are what determine the character of a routing protocol.

Under some algorithms each node has complete knowledge of the network. That needs large local storage and enough processor to search the tables quickly, since it must be done for each packet, and updates usually carry only changes, because passing everything would consume the network's capacity. These algorithms have problems, because the only way information travels is across the network and the propagation time is not trivial, so each node's view is a correct historical view of the network at some time in the past. Those inconsistencies can cause circular routes, where a packet enters a closed path until its time to live expires and it is discarded. Other algorithms know only a subset of the network and are used hierarchically, knowing their own area completely but going to one particular place to leave it.

The protocols in use at the time were described one by one. Static routing, the document says not to laugh, is probably the most reliable, easiest to implement and least likely to get one into trouble for a small network, but it should be used in the middle of a network with extreme caution, because routers passing dynamic information can be confused by conflicting static and dynamic routes.

RIP is a distance vector protocol based on the Xerox Network System and adapted for IP, used by many routers and many BSD Unix systems. It works best for networks of small diameter over links of equal speed, because its metric is the hop count. A hop count of 16 is defined as infinity in RIP, meaning the link is down, so hosts separated by more than 15 gateways in the RIP space cannot communicate. The other problem with hop counts is that differences in link speed are not reflected, so a one hop satellite link with half a second of delay at 56 kilobits would be preferred over a two hop T1 connection, and the resulting congestion makes matters worse. RIP was originally poorly documented, and people read the BSD source to find out how it worked, until it was finally documented in RFC 1058.

Hello was designed and implemented in an experimental software router called a Fuzzball running on a PDP-11. It has no wide usage, but it was the protocol formerly used on the initial NSFNET backbone. Its data is similar to RIP, a list of networks and their metrics, but the metric is milliseconds of delay, which lets it work over links of various speeds and behave better when congested. Because measuring delay on a link is hard, Hello routers pass time around the network, and in a nationwide network they maintain synchronised time within milliseconds.

EGP is not strictly a routing protocol but a reachability protocol: it says which networks can be reached through which gateway, but not how good the connection is. It is the standard by which gateways exchange reachability information with the core gateways, and is generally used between autonomous systems. A metric is passed around, ranging from 0 to 255 with smaller values considered better, though its use is not formally standardised.

The gated program was written to solve the problem of how regional and campus networks speaking RIP could interoperate with the DDN and NSFNET speaking EGP. It talks RIP to RIP-speaking hosts, EGP to EGP speakers and Hello to Hello speakers, and its configuration files can filter the conversion, so that a rogue network appearing in a site's RIP space is not passed on to the other side. The catch is metric conversion: RIP measures in hops, Hello in milliseconds and EGP in arbitrary small numbers, and infinity is 16 to RIP, around 30000 to Hello and 8 to the DDN with EGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers pass information about the network to each other, and the way they do it decides how well packets get through. The document walks through the methods in use, from writing the routes out by hand to counting the gateways a packet has to cross.

sections.title: Names, Addresses and Mail Reflectors
sections.content:
All routing across the network is done by means of the IP address in the packet. Since humans find it difficult to remember addresses like 128.174.5.50, a symbolic name register was set up at the Network Information Center, where people would say that they would like their host to be named uiucuxc. Machines connected across the nation would connect to the center in the middle of the night, check the modification dates on the hosts file, and copy it locally if it had changed. With the advent of workstations and micros, the hosts file had to be changed nightly, which was labour intensive and consumed a lot of network bandwidth. RFC 1034 and a number of others describe the Domain Name Service, a distributed database system for mapping names into addresses.

The document looks closely at what is in a name. An address specifies a particular connection on a specific network, so if the machine moves the address changes. A machine can have one or more names and one or more network addresses on different networks. Names point to something that does useful work, while IP addresses point to an interface on that provider. A name is a purely symbolic representation of a list of addresses, so if a machine moves to a different network the addresses change but the name can stay the same.

Domain names are tree structured, with the root of the tree at the right. In the example uxc.cso.uiuc.edu, uxc is a machine with a purely arbitrary name, inside the subdomains of the University of Illinois, which is registered with edu, the set of educational institutions. To resolve a name, a resolver on the user's machine contacts a root name server, which knows who handles the first level domains. From the root server the resolver learns who provides the edu service, contacts that name server, which supplies a list of addresses of servers for the subdomains, and repeats the process until the final subdomain returns a list of addresses of interfaces on the host in question. The user's machine then chooses which of those addresses to use.

A group may apply for its own domain name in a manner similar to IP address allocation. The only requirement is that the requestor have two machines reachable from the Internet to act as name servers for that domain, and those servers need not be in any particular place. The biggest problem is that someone must do maintenance on the database, and if the machine is not convenient that might not be done in a timely fashion.

The BIND server implements the Internet name server for UNIX systems, and replaces the hosts file. Its most important advantage is that it frees a host from relying on the hosts file being up to date and complete. BIND can also supply mail forwarding information for interior hosts that are not directly reachable from the Internet, either because they sit on non-advertised networks or because they are not connected to an IP network at all.

The way most people keep up to date with network news is through subscription to mail reflectors, also known as mail exploders. A reflector is a special electronic mailbox which, when it receives a message, resends it to a list of other mailboxes, which in effect creates a discussion group on a topic. To subscribe, the general format is to find the address of the reflector and append the string -REQUEST to the mailbox name rather than the host name. The document points out the weakness of the scheme: you have to know the list exists first, so it suggests reading the mail on one list and becoming familiar with the others. A registration service for reflectors is provided in files held at the Network Information Center.

Before a local network can be connected to the Internet it must be allocated a unique IP address, and these are allocated by SRI-NIC. IP addresses are 32 bits long and are usually written as four decimal numbers separated by periods, each number being the value of an octet. Networks were differentiated into class A, B and C, with the high order bits in the first octet coding for the address format: a few large networks, a reasonable number of medium ones and a large number of small ones. There are also class D for multicast and class E for experimental use.

In the past, sites requiring multiple network addresses requested multiple discrete addresses, usually class C, because much of the software available, notably 4.2BSD, could not deal with subnetted addresses. Some nodes have a limited capability to store and exchange routing information, limited to about 700 networks, so the document suggests that any campus announce no more than two discrete network numbers. Subnetting allows one address to be announced to the Internet while a set of addresses is used on the campus, with a different mask used in each place. The document ends this part with a warning that not all systems know how to do subnetting: some 4.2BSD systems require additional software, while 4.3BSD systems subnet as released, and other devices and operating systems vary in the problems they have dealing with subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: People use names, machines use numbers, and something has to translate between them. The document explains the tree of names, the file of numbers that used to be copied around the world, and the trick of subnetting that let one site use many numbers while announcing only one.

sections.title: The Problems of 1989
sections.content:
The document lists a number of problems with the Internet, with solutions ranging from software changes to long term research projects.

The first is the number of networks. When the Internet was designed it was to have about 50 connected networks, and with the explosion of networking the number was approaching 1000. The software in a group of critical gateways, called the core gateways, was not able to pass or store much more than that, and in the short term core reallocation and recoding raised the number slightly.

The second is routing. Along with the sheer mass of the data needed to route packets to a large number of networks, there are problems with the updating, stability and optimality of the routing algorithms. Much research was being done, but the optimal solution was still years away. In most cases the routing in use worked, but sub-optimally and sometimes unpredictably. The document names OSPF, then known as OSPFIGP, as the current best hope for a good routing protocol, expected to be generally available from many router manufacturers within a year.

The third is trust. Gateways exchange network routing information, and most gateways accept on faith that the information provided about the state of the network is correct. In the past this was not a big problem, since most gateways belonged to a single administrative entity. With multiple wide area networks under different administrations, a rogue gateway somewhere in the net could cripple the Internet, and design work was under way on both that problem and the problem of providing enough information to route data between multiply connected networks.

The fourth is capacity and congestion. Some portions of the Internet were very congested during the busy part of the day, and growth was dramatic, with some networks experiencing growth in traffic in excess of 20 percent per month. Additional bandwidth was planned, but delivery and budgets might not allow supply to keep up.

A separate section covers what was wrong with Berkeley Unix, which had been funded by DARPA to modify the Unix system to support the Internet protocols. Earlier versions such as BSD 4.2 had good support for the basic protocols, which allowed them to perform nicely on IP Ethernets and smaller Internets, but had deficiencies when connected to complicated networks. Most of these problems were resolved under BSD 4.3, and since Berkeley's release was the springboard from which many vendors launched their own Unix implementations, many of them were still based on 4.2 and still had the 4.2 problems.

Three scenarios are worked through. ICMP redirects are ignored by BSD 4.2, which creates more stress on the gateways and the local network, since for every packet sent the gateway sends a packet back to the originator. BSD 4.3 uses the redirect to update its routing tables, keeps the route until it times out and then reverts, which is far better than one reply per packet. The second is trailers, where the headers are put at the end of the block instead of the beginning; they were never standardised and most gateways do not know to look for the routing information there, so short files work but long ones seem to hang, and on 4.2 trailers are a boot option that should be off when using the Internet, while 4.3 negotiates them and uses them only on the local net. The third is retransmission, where BSD 4.2 retransmitted quickly and often, which is what you want on a low delay network of large bandwidth but is too aggressive on a longer delay network with scarce bandwidth. BSD 4.3 does better by firing off a few retransmissions really quickly and then backing off very quickly, and it allows about four minutes before giving up. The document notes that an even better version of the algorithm was developed by Van Jacobson and integrated into the later releases of BSD 4.3.

The last scenario is the time to live. TTL was designed to prevent packets caught in routing loops from being passed forever, and because the definition bears some likeness to the RIP hop count, some misguided systems set the TTL field to 15, since the unreachable flag in RIP is 16. No network could have more than 15 hops that way, and the RIP space where hops are limited ends when RIP is not used as a routing protocol, so it is quite easy for a packet to require more than 15 hops. Such machines reach some places but not others even though the routing information appears correct, and solving the problem typically requires kernel patches.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists what worried it most: too many networks for the core routers to handle, routing that worked badly, gateways that believed whatever they were told, and links that were simply too full. It ends with the kinds of bug that made Unix systems behave oddly on a real network.
